short: Lecture 14 · Active Instagram use, self-esteem & well-being

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Find the FIRST formal hypothesis exactly as the authors state it.
items.model: H1: More active Instagram use will be associated with higher self-esteem, with intensity as a mediator.
items.why: The formal hypotheses come at the end of the literature review. The abstract gives a simplified version that leaves the mediator out.

items.label: Variables in the mediation model
items.prompt: Name the predictor (X), the mediator (M) and the TWO outcome variables (Y).
items.model: X = active Instagram use; M = intensity of Instagram use; Y = self-esteem and well-being.
items.why: A mediator sits in the middle: X → M → Y. Here active use → intensity → self-esteem / well-being.

items.label: Conceptual definition (intensity)
items.prompt: Find the sentence that gives a CONCEPTUAL definition of the mediator.
items.model: User intensity = the strength of a person's emotional connection to SNS content.
items.why: A conceptual definition says what the concept MEANS. The operational definition (how it was measured) comes later in the Method.

items.label: Operational definition (intensity)
items.prompt: How was the mediator actually MEASURED? Find the sentence naming the instrument and where it came from.
items.model: The Intensity Scale, adapted from Ellison et al. (2007) for Instagram.
items.why: The next sentences describe its Likert items. Any of them is accepted.

items.label: Theoretical framework
items.prompt: Which THEORY do the authors use to explain why intensity should matter?
items.model: Social capital theory: intense, active use builds social capital (belonging, connectedness), which raises self-esteem and well-being.
items.why: The framework is named in the literature review and again in the Discussion.

items.label: Sampling method
items.prompt: The abstract calls this a 'snowball sample'. Based on the METHOD section, what kind of sample is it really?
options: A simple random sample of undergraduates drawn from US college enrolment lists
A convenience (volunteer) sample from social-media posts and extra-credit students
A snowball sample in which each participant recruited further college friends
A stratified sample with equal numbers of students from each US region
items.ans: A convenience (volunteer) sample from social-media posts and extra-credit students
items.model: A convenience (volunteer) sample, not truly snowball or random.
items.why: Recruitment was through Facebook/Instagram posts and course credit at one university. Nothing in the Method describes participants recruiting other participants (snowballing), and nothing is random.

items.label: Recruitment incentive
items.prompt: Find the sentence showing that some participants were given an incentive to take part.
items.model: Students at one New England university were recruited in exchange for extra credit.
items.why: Incentives and a single-university subgroup are possible sources of sampling bias.

items.label: Recruited vs final sample
items.prompt: How many questionnaires were submitted, and how many were analysed?
items.model: 411 submitted, 359 usable (52 excluded for incomplete data).
items.why: Always compare the number recruited with the number analysed. Here about 13% of responses were dropped.

items.label: Research design
items.prompt: Which best describes the design?
options: Quasi-experiment comparing active vs passive users
items.model: Cross-sectional correlational survey.
items.why: One online survey at one time point; nothing was manipulated. Mediation analysis doesn't change the design: it's still correlational.

items.label: Reliability
items.prompt: Which statistic do the authors report as evidence of RELIABILITY for their scales, and what is the LOWEST value?
items.model: Cronbach's α (internal consistency): .73 (active use), .83 (intensity), .89 (self-esteem), .86 (well-being). Lowest = .73.
items.why: Cronbach's α above about .70 is usually treated as acceptable internal consistency.

items.label: Reliability vs validity mix-up
items.prompt: One sentence in the Method claims something is evidence of RELIABILITY when it actually describes VALIDITY. Find it.
items.model: 'The scale has proven to accurately measure the two components of subjective well-being… exemplifying the measure's reliability.'
items.why: Accurately measuring what it's supposed to measure is VALIDITY. Reliability is consistency (e.g. Cronbach's α).

items.label: Citation error
items.prompt: One scale is cited to the wrong source (the source given is actually the paper for a DIFFERENT scale used in this study). Find it.
items.model: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale is cited as Diener et al. (1985), but Diener et al. (1985) is the Satisfaction with Life Scale.
items.why: Check that each measure is cited to the paper that developed it. The reference list confirms Diener et al. (1985) is 'The satisfaction with life scale'.

items.label: Dropped variable
items.prompt: Find the sentence showing the authors collected data on a variable but chose NOT to analyse it in the Results.
items.model: Passive use data were collected but treated as beyond the goals of the study.
items.why: It later appears in the Discussion, where passive use is ALSO positively related to self-esteem and well-being. That doesn't fit the theory they describe in the Introduction (passive use should be harmful).

items.label: Result that contradicts the theory
items.prompt: Find the result reported in the Discussion that doesn't fit the theory presented in the literature review.
items.model: Passive use was also positively correlated with self-esteem (r = .13) and well-being (r = .19).
items.why: The literature review says passive use leads to lower self-esteem (2.13), but here passive use goes WITH higher self-esteem and well-being.

items.label: Strength of the correlations
items.prompt: How strong is the correlation between active Instagram use and self-esteem (r = .13)?
options: Strong and positive, so active use explains most of the variation in self-esteem
Weak and positive: active use shares under 2% of the variance with self-esteem
Moderate and positive: active use explains about a quarter of the variance
Not significant, because the p value is above the .05 level the authors set
items.ans: Weak and positive: active use shares under 2% of the variance with self-esteem
items.model: Weak and positive: about 2% of the variance in self-esteem
items.why: r = .13 is significant (p = .017) but weak: r² ≈ .017, so active use shares under 2% of variance with self-esteem. A large sample makes small effects significant.

items.label: What the mediation result means
items.prompt: The direct effect of active use on self-esteem was NOT significant (c' = 0.08, p = .401), but the indirect effect through intensity WAS. What does this mean?
options: Active use directly causes higher self-esteem, and intensity is irrelevant to it
Statistically, the link from active use to self-esteem runs through intensity
There is no relationship of any kind between active use and self-esteem
The hypothesis was rejected because the direct effect was not significant
items.ans: Statistically, the link from active use to self-esteem runs through intensity
items.model: The link between active use and self-esteem goes through intensity (full mediation), statistically
items.why: Once intensity is accounted for, active use adds nothing on its own. But in cross-sectional data this is a statistical pattern, not proof of a causal chain.

items.label: Causal overclaim
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the DISCUSSION that uses causal language the design can't support.
items.model: '…the ways in which young adults engage with online content have the ability to significantly impact how they feel about themselves.'
items.why: 'Impact' implies cause. A one-time correlational survey can't show that Instagram use CHANGES self-esteem. The authors themselves admit this later (12.11).

items.label: Limitations
items.prompt: Find the sentence where the authors admit the design can't show cause and effect.
items.model: Because of the nature of the research, causality can't be asserted.
items.why: The limitations paragraph has three: no causality, weak effect sizes, and active/passive categories that aren't mutually exclusive.

items.label: Measurement limitation
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining WHY the active-use measure is a problem.
items.model: Active and passive use aren't mutually exclusive: users can be both, even in the same session.
items.why: A measurement limitation: the scale treats active and passive as separate, but behaviour overlaps.

items.label: Generalisability
items.prompt: Give TWO features of the sample that limit generalisability (the authors don't mention them).
items.model: e.g. only US undergraduates (mean age 20), about two-thirds female, self-selected volunteers from social media plus one university's extra-credit pool.
items.why: The authors list limitations about causality and measurement but say nothing about who the sample represents. Spotting what is NOT said is part of critical reading.

items.label: Future research
items.prompt: Name ONE method the authors suggest future research should use instead of surveys.
items.model: Experiments, interviews or direct behavioural observation.
items.why: Suggested because surveys rely on self-report and can't establish cause.

items.label: Ethics
items.prompt: Find the evidence that the study received ethical approval.
items.model: Approved by the university's Institutional Review Board (IRB).
items.why: An IRB is an ethics committee. Note there's no detail on consent or debriefing in the text.
